pros: Lower memory than BFS for balanced graphs (O(log V) vs O(V))
Natural for recursive backtracking problems (maze, puzzles, constraints)
Classifies edges (tree, back, forward, cross) — crucial for many algorithms
Foundation for topological sort in DAGs (post-order gives reverse topo order)
Enables cycle detection via back edge identification
Powers Tarjan's algorithm for SCC, articulation points, bridges
Simple recursive implementation (few lines of code)
Can be used for exhaustive search in decision trees and game trees
Discovers deep solutions quickly (good when solutions are deep)
Works with both directed and undirected graphs
Can record discovery/finishing times for rich graph analysis
Iterative version avoids stack overflow while preserving depth-first order
cons: Recursive implementation risks stack overflow on deep graphs (e.g., V=10⁶ path)
Does NOT find shortest path (unlike BFS)
May go down infinite depth in infinite graphs (mitigated by depth limit)
Can get stuck in deep unfruitful branches (no heuristic like A*)
Iterative version is more complex to implement with correct post-order
Stack space can be O(V) for skewed graphs (e.g., linked list, star)
Cannot be parallelized easily due to sequential nature
Memory overhead for recursion metadata in some languages
Less intuitive for shortest-distance problems than BFS
Not suitable for distributed graph processing without modification
Backtracking can be expensive if solutions are shallow and graph is deep
Depth-limited and iterative deepening add complexity over basic BFS
